title: Come to the Waters: An Everlasting Covenant
summary: God calls everyone who is thirsty and has no money to come and receive food and drink for free, and asks why people spend their wages on what cannot satisfy. He offers an everlasting covenant based on the loyal love promised to David, and urges the wicked to seek him and return while he may be found, because he freely pardons and his thoughts are higher than human thoughts. His word will accomplish its purpose like rain that waters the earth, and his people will go out with joy while creation sings.
story: Chapter 55 closes the great section of Isaiah that began in chapter 40 with “Comfort, comfort My people.” Chapter 53 showed the Servant bearing sin; chapter 54 showed Zion restored as a mother of many; now the invitation goes out to anyone who will come. The section began with God's word that stands forever (40:8) and ends with God's word that does not return empty (55:11), a deliberate frame. After this, chapters 56 to 66 turn to the life of the restored community.
historical:
The chapter's invitation to go out with joy (verse 12) fits the period after Cyrus of Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC and allowed Judeans to return, whether these words were spoken then or foreseen. Not all exiles wanted to go. Many had settled in Babylon, as Jeremiah had told them to (Jeremiah 29:4-7), and records from the period show Judeans doing business and holding land there. For them the chapter's question in verse 2, why spend money on what does not satisfy, may have had a concrete edge: comfort in Babylon against the call to return to a ruined homeland.

The promise tied to David (verses 3 and 4) came to a people with no king. The last reigning Davidic king, Zedekiah, had been blinded and taken to Babylon (2 Kings 25:7), and his exiled predecessor Jehoiachin was released from prison but never restored to his throne (2 Kings 25:27-30). God's covenant with David in 2 Samuel 7 had promised a house and a throne forever. The question hanging over the exile was what had become of that promise.
cultural:
Verse 1 sounds like a street vendor calling out wares in a market: water, grain, wine, and milk, the basic foods of the ancient Mediterranean diet. Wine and milk together stood for abundance, the good life of a fertile land. The twist is that the vendor asks nothing. In a world where most people lived close to subsistence and spent their labor to buy bread, the offer of rich food without cost was startling.

Rain and snow (verse 10) were not background weather to Israel. The land depended on seasonal rains, the early rains of autumn and the late rains of spring, and a failed rain meant famine. Snow fell rarely except on the heights and in the north, and its runoff fed springs. The image of rain that does not return until it has done its work would have been deeply felt by farmers who watched the sky. The thornbush and brier of verse 13 are the signs of a cursed, neglected land (Genesis 3:18; Isaiah 5:6); their replacement by cypress and myrtle signals the curse reversed.
literary: The chapter is built as a series of invitations, heavy with imperatives: come, buy, eat, listen, incline, seek, call, return. Verses 1 to 5 are a covenant invitation, first to the individual thirsty person and then widening to the nations. Verses 6 and 7 are a call to repentance. Verses 8 to 11 give the ground for it in two comparisons: God's thoughts are as high above ours as the heavens are above the earth, and his word works as surely as rain. Verses 12 and 13 close with a joyful procession in which mountains sing and trees clap, language that echoes the exodus and the new creation promised throughout chapters 40 to 55.

outline.t: Come, all who are thirsty: food without cost
An everlasting covenant: the love promised to David
Seek the LORD while he may be found
Higher thoughts, and a word that does not return empty
Going out with joy: creation sings

doctrines.note: The offer is free: “without money and without cost” (verse 1). What satisfies cannot be bought, only received. Salvation here is both gift and summons, since the invitation is to come, listen, and return.

“Let the wicked man forsake his own way” and return to the LORD, who “will freely pardon” (verse 7). Repentance is a change of way and of thought, and it is met not with reluctant tolerance but with abundant forgiveness.
God's word goes out like rain and accomplishes his purpose (verses 10 and 11). Scripture is not merely information about God but his active speech, which does what he sends it to do.

words.note: Salach, to forgive or pardon. In the Old Testament this verb has only God as its subject: people forgive one another with other words, but salach is always God's pardon. In verse 7 it is intensified by a word meaning to multiply or be abundant, hence “freely pardon” or abundantly pardon.

Chesed, loyal covenant love. Verse 3 speaks of “My loving devotion promised to David,” literally the faithful mercies of David, the steadfast love God pledged in 2 Samuel 7 when he promised David a lasting house and throne. Isaiah offers that same loyal love to all who come.

Berit, covenant, a binding relationship sealed by oath. Here it is an everlasting covenant made with the listeners (verse 3). Scholars discuss whether the chapter transfers the royal promises of David to the whole people, or renews them in the expectation of a coming Davidic king; the New Testament reads them in the second way.

christ: In Acts 13:34 Paul, preaching in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, quotes verse 3 in its Greek form to argue that God's promises to David are fulfilled in the resurrection of Jesus, the Davidic king who will not see decay. The chapter's invitation to the thirsty is taken up by Jesus, who stood up at the Feast of Tabernacles and called anyone who is thirsty to come to him and drink (John 7:37), and Revelation ends with the same call to take the water of life without cost (Revelation 22:17). The link with David is predictive in Isaiah's own terms; the links with water are thematic, the same invitation extended.

hard.q: If God's thoughts are higher than ours, can we really know anything about him?
hard.a: Verses 8 and 9 are sometimes used to shut down hard questions: God's ways are mysterious, so stop asking. The context points elsewhere. The contrast comes right after verse 7, where the wicked are told God will freely pardon. God's thoughts are higher than ours especially in his readiness to forgive, which outruns human ideas of fairness and payback. That does not mean God is unknowable; the same passage says his word comes down like rain and accomplishes his purpose, which means he makes himself known. The church's tradition has held both: God is beyond full human comprehension, yet truly known where he reveals himself. The verses invite humility, not silence.

questions: Verse 2 asks why we spend money and labor on what does not satisfy. What in your life gets that kind of spending?
Why do you think God's higher thoughts in verse 8 are connected so closely with his readiness to pardon in verse 7?
The chapter says God's word will not return empty. Where have you seen Scripture do something in a person over time that you did not expect?
